domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)   # row index of A, and index into r and q
    j: dim in [0, M)   # column index of A, and index into p and s

data:
    # Matrix A of size N x M, stored row-major as in the C code A[i][j].
    A[i, j]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * M + j

    # Input vectors.
    p[j]: in  DATA_TYPE = j       # length M
    r[i]: in  DATA_TYPE = i       # length N

    # Output vectors.
    q[i]: out DATA_TYPE = i       # length N, q = A * p
    s[j]: out DATA_TYPE = j       # length M, s = A^T * r

parameters:
    # Problem sizes (match PolyBench N and M).
    N: int        # number of rows of A, length of r and q
    M: int        # number of columns of A, length of p and s

    # Tunable performance parameters.
    TI: int       # tile size along i (rows), e.g., 64
    TJ: int       # tile size along j (cols), e.g., 64
    VEC_J: int    # SIMD width along j, e.g., 4 (double) or 8 (float)
    NUM_THREADS: int  # maximum number of worker threads

computation:
    # 1. Initialize s to zero over its M entries.
    #    This matches the first loop in the Exo kernel:
    #      for i in 0..m-1: s[i] = 0
    for j in [0, M):
        s[j] = 0

    # 2. Main BiCG computation in a single pass over A.
    #
    #    Semantics (per the original Exo kernel):
    #      - For each row i, initialize q[i] to 0.
    #      - Then for each column j:
    #          s[j] += r[i] * A[i, j]   # contributes to s = A^T r
    #          q[i] += A[i, j] * p[j]   # contributes to q = A p
    #
    #    Final results:
    #      q[i] = sum_{j=0}^{M-1} A[i, j] * p[j]
    #      s[j] = sum_{i=0}^{N-1} r[i]   * A[i, j]
    for i in [0, N):
        q[i] = 0
        for j in [0, M):
            s[j] += r[i] * A[i, j]
            q[i] += A[i, j] * p[j]

optimization:
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Cache blocking of the main (i, j) nest
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Block both the i- and j-dimensions in the main BiCG loop so that each
    # A-tile of size TI x TJ, together with the relevant slices of p, q, r,
    # and s, fits into L1/L2 cache.
    #
    # Conceptually transforms:
    #   for i in [0, N):
    #     q[i] = 0
    #     for j in [0, M):
    #       s[j] += r[i] * A[i, j]
    #       q[i] += A[i, j] * p[j]
    #
    # into a tiled form:
    #   for I in [0, ceil(N / TI)):
    #     for J in [0, ceil(M / TJ)):
    #       for i in [I*TI, min((I+1)*TI, N)):
    #         if first time this i is seen: q[i] = 0
    #         for j in [J*TJ, min((J+1)*TJ, M)):
    #           s[j] += r[i] * A[i, j]
    #           q[i] += A[i, j] * p[j]
    #
    # preserving the exact mathematical result.
    block(i, I, TI)   # tile the row dimension of the main BiCG loop
    block(j, J, TJ)   # tile the column dimension of the main BiCG loop
    hoist(I)          # move I outermost around the (i, j) body
    hoist(J)          # move J just inside I, yielding I -> J -> i -> j

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelization across row tiles I
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallelize the outermost tile loop I. Each worker thread processes a
    # disjoint subset of row tiles I, giving coarse-grain parallelism.
    #
    # Data dependencies:
    #   - q[i] is a per-row result:
    #         q[i] = sum_j A[i, j] * p[j]
    #     Each row i belongs to exactly one I-tile, so only one thread ever
    #     writes to a given q[i]. No synchronization is needed for q.
    #
    #   - s[j] is a reduction over the i-dimension:
    #         s[j] = sum_i r[i] * A[i, j]
    #     When I is parallelized, different threads compute contributions to
    #     the same s[j] from different row tiles I. These must be combined
    #     via a reduction:
    #
    #       #pragma omp parallel for reduction(+: s[0:M])
    #       for I in ...
    #         ...
    #
    #     A typical implementation keeps a private s_partial[j] per thread
    #     and reduces them into s[j] at the end of the parallel region. The
    #     extra scratch space is O(M * NUM_THREADS); for realistic workloads
    #     with N >> NUM_THREADS it remains well below 50% of the original
    #     N*M A-storage and satisfies the memory-growth constraint.
    parallelize(I)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # SIMD vectorization along the inner column dimension j
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # After blocking, j is the innermost loop inside a tile (I, J) and
    # indexes:
    #   - the contiguous dimension of row-major A (A[i, j]),
    #   - the contiguous vector p[j],
    #   - and the contiguous vector s[j].
    #
    # Vectorizing this innermost loop by VEC_J lets the compiler map:
    #   A[i, j  : j+VEC_J],
    #   p[   j  : j+VEC_J],
    #   s[   j  : j+VEC_J]
    # to SIMD registers. For each i, q[i] is kept in a scalar accumulator
    # (in a register) and updated using horizontal reductions over the SIMD
    # products A[i, j:*] * p[j:*].
    #
    # This improves throughput while preserving scalar semantics.
    vectorize(j, VEC_J)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Scalar replacement / accumulation variables
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Use scalar temporaries to reduce redundant memory traffic:
    #
    #   - Hoist r[i] out of the innermost j-loop into a scalar "r_i"
    #     for each i in a tile:
    #         r_i = r[i]
    #         for j in tile:
    #             s[j] += r_i * A[i, j]
    #
    #   - For each (I, i) within the tile, accumulate q[i] in a scalar
    #     temporary "tmp_q" inside the j-loop and write it back once:
    #         tmp_q = 0
    #         for j in tile:
    #             tmp_q += A[i, j] * p[j]
    #         q[i] += tmp_q    # or q[i] = tmp_q if only one tile J per i
    #
    # These transformations are algebraically neutral; they only change
    # where values are stored (register vs. memory).
    # (Expressed as high-level hints rather than named primitives.)
    #   hoist_load(r[i] -> r_i)
    #   accumulate_in_register(q[i] over j -> tmp_q)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Parallel and vectorized initialization of s
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------
    # The initialization loop for s:
    #   for j in [0, M): s[j] = 0
    # writes each element exactly once and does not depend on any other
    # data. It can be parallelized and vectorized independently:
    parallelize(j)          # applied to the s-initialization loop
    vectorize(j, VEC_J)     # SIMD zeroing over s[j]

```text
domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)          # rows of A and q, indices of r
    j: dim in [0, M)          # columns of A and s, indices of p

data:
    # A ∈ R^{N×M}, stored row-major (PolyBench layout)
    A[i, j]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * M + j

    # Input vectors
    r[i]: in  DATA_TYPE = i          # length N, contiguous
    p[j]: in  DATA_TYPE = j          # length M, contiguous

    # Output vectors (overwritten by the kernel)
    s[j]: out DATA_TYPE = j          # length M, contiguous
    q[i]: out DATA_TYPE = i          # length N, contiguous

parameters:
    # Tuning parameters for a 32‑core x64 machine
    TI: int, TI > 0                  # tile size in i (rows of A), e.g. 64–256
    TJ: int, TJ > 0                  # tile size in j (columns of A), multiple of VEC_WIDTH
    VEC_WIDTH: int, VEC_WIDTH > 0    # SIMD width (# of elements), e.g. 4 (AVX2 double) or 8 (AVX‑512 double)
    UNROLL_J: int, UNROLL_J > 0      # unroll factor inside the innermost j loop
    NT: int, 1 ≤ NT ≤ 64             # number of worker threads

computation:
    # BiCG computes:
    #   s[j] = sum_{i=0}^{N-1} r[i] * A[i, j]      (s = Aᵀ r)
    #   q[i] = sum_{j=0}^{M-1} A[i, j] * p[j]      (q = A p)
    # The code below matches the Exo kernel exactly.

    # 1. Initialize s to zero over its M entries
    INIT_S:
    for j in [0, M):
        s[j] = 0.0

    # 2. Main BiCG computation: fused use of A to form both s and q
    #
    #    For each row i:
    #      - q[i] is initialized to 0
    #      - we walk across all columns j
    #      - we update:
    #           s[j] += r[i] * A[i, j]
    #           q[i] += A[i, j] * p[j]
    #
    #    At the end:
    #      s[j] = Σ_i r[i] * A[i, j]
    #      q[i] = Σ_j A[i, j] * p[j]
    MAIN:
    for i in [0, N):
        q[i] = 0.0
        for j in [0, M):
            s[j] += r[i] * A[i, j]
            q[i] += A[i, j] * p[j]

optimization:
    # 1. Hoist loop‑invariant and reuse‑able values into registers
    #
    #    Within MAIN:
    #      - For each i, load r_i = r[i] once before the inner j loop.
    #      - Inside the innermost loop, load a_ij = A[i, j] once and reuse it
    #        for both updates:
    #            tmp = a_ij
    #            s[j] += r_i * tmp
    #            q[i] += tmp * p[j]
    #
    #    This reduces memory traffic and redundant multiplies while preserving
    #    the exact mathematical result.

    # 2. Tile and SIMD‑vectorize the j‑dimension (contiguous in memory).
    #
    #    Rationale:
    #      - j indexes the fast (contiguous) dimension of A, p, and s.
    #      - Tiling j improves cache locality for A’s rows and for s / p.
    #      - Mapping j to SIMD lanes yields efficient use of AVX2/AVX‑512.
    block(j, J, TJ)                # j = J * TJ + j_in, TJ tuned to fit L1 and be a multiple of VEC_WIDTH
    vectorize(j, VEC_WIDTH)        # map inner j_in loop to SIMD lanes
    unroll(j, UNROLL_J)            # unroll within the SIMDized j loop for ILP

    # 3. Tile and parallelize the i‑dimension, with a reduction onto s.
    #
    #    Rationale:
    #      - Different i-iterations update different q[i] (no dependency),
    #        but they all contribute to every s[j], so s is a reduction over i.
    #      - We distribute tiles of rows (I) across threads and use
    #        per-thread partial sums for s to avoid write contention.
    #
    #    Transformation:
    block(i, I, TI)                # i = I * TI + i_in, choose TI for good per-thread work and L2 locality
    hoist(I)                       # make I the outermost loop in MAIN
    parallelize(I)                 # execute different I-tiles on different threads (up to NT threads)

    #    Correctness of s under parallelization:
    #      - Introduce a temporary buffer s_priv[t, j] of shape [NT, M]
    #        (DATA_TYPE), initialized to zero. This adds at most NT * M
    #        elements, well under the 50% extra memory budget since A
    #        dominates the footprint.
    #      - In the parallelized MAIN:
    #           * Each worker thread t processes a disjoint subset of I-tiles.
    #           * It accumulates into its private s_priv[t, j] instead of s[j]:
    #                 s_priv[t, j] += r[i] * A[i, j]
    #           * It still writes q[i] directly, since each i belongs
    #             to exactly one thread.
    #      - After all I-tiles are done, perform a sequential (or
    #        parallel over j) reduction:
    #             for j in [0, M):
    #                 s[j] = sum_{t=0}^{NT-1} s_priv[t, j]
    #      - This realizes:
    #             s[j] = Σ_i r[i] * A[i, j]
    #        exactly, with only a benign reordering of floating‑point
    #        additions.

    # 4. Parallelize embarrassingly-parallel 1D loops over j.
    #
    #    The initialization of s has no cross‑iteration dependencies,
    #    so we can safely parallelize it across j:
    parallelize(j) on INIT_S       # simple 1D partition of j in [0, M)
    #    The reduction loop over j that combines s_priv[t, j] into s[j]
    #    can likewise be parallelized over j if desired, as each s[j]
    #    is independent.

    # 5. (Optional) Cache‑friendly loop order after tiling.
    #
    #    After applying block(i, I, TI) and block(j, J, TJ), use the
    #    loop order:
    #
    #        for I in [0, ceil(N / TI)):        # parallel over I
    #          for J in [0, ceil(M / TJ)):
    #            for i_in in [0, TI):
    #              for j_in in [0, TJ):         # vectorized & unrolled
    #                 ... BiCG update ...
    #
    #    This order:
    #      - Keeps accesses to A[i, j] row‑major and contiguous in j_in.
    #      - Reuses p[j] and the per-thread s_priv[t, j] within J-tiles.
    #      - Provides coarse-grain parallel work units (I-tiles) for
    #        good scaling on 32 cores.
```

```text
domain:
    # Problem dimensions: A is n×m, q and r are length n, s and p are length m.
    i: dim in [0, n)
    j: dim in [0, m)
    # Intra-tile indices for rows and columns (used only in the optimized schedule).
    ii: dim in [0, TI)
    jj: dim in [0, TJ)

data:
    # Row-major matrix: A[i, j] = A_base[i * m + j]
    A[i, j]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * m + j

    # Vectors, all stored contiguously.
    p[j]: in    DATA_TYPE = (j) -> j
    r[i]: in    DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i
    s[j]: out   DATA_TYPE = (j) -> j   # overwritten: computes s = Aᵀ r
    q[i]: out   DATA_TYPE = (i) -> i   # overwritten: computes q = A p

    # Tile-local temporaries used in the optimized schedule.
    # q_tile[ii] holds partial sums of q for a small block of rows (size TI).
    # s_tile[jj] holds partial sums of s for a small block of columns (size TJ).
    #
    # Extra memory is TI + TJ elements. The original footprint is
    #   |A| + |s| + |q| + |p| + |r| = n·m + 2m + 2n
    # so the relative overhead (TI + TJ)/(n·m + 2m + 2n) is ≤ (n + m)/(n·m + 2m + 2n) < 0.4
    # for all n, m ≥ 1 — well under the required 50% bound.
    q_tile[ii]: local DATA_TYPE = (ii) -> ii
    s_tile[jj]: local DATA_TYPE = (jj) -> jj

parameters:
    # Tuning parameters (chosen so tiles fit in cache and match SIMD width).
    TI: int  # tile size in the row (i) dimension, e.g., 32–128
    TJ: int  # tile size in the column (j) dimension, e.g., 64–256
    VJ: int  # SIMD width for column-wise vectorization; must divide TJ (or its inner remainder)

computation:
    # BiCG kernel semantics, expressed as two matrix–vector products:
    #
    #   s = Aᵀ r    where   s[j] = Σ_i A[i, j] * r[i]
    #   q = A p     where   q[i] = Σ_j A[i, j] * p[j]
    #
    # The Exo kernel initializes s and q to zero and then accumulates these sums.
    # These assignments fully specify the mathematical result; the schedule below
    # fuses and tiles the loops while preserving these sums (up to FP reordering).

    S: for j:
        s[j] = sum(i, A[i, j] * r[i])

    Q: for i:
        q[i] = sum(j, A[i, j] * p[j])

optimization:
    # 1) Fuse the two reductions so we traverse A only once.
    #    After fusion, each (i, j) pair contributes simultaneously to s[j] and q[i]:
    #
    #    for i in [0, n), j in [0, m):
    #        s[j] += A[i, j] * r[i]
    #        q[i] += A[i, j] * p[j]
    #
    # This preserves the sums defining S and Q but halves the number of A loads.
    fuse(S, Q)  # custom: fuse S and Q into one double loop over (i, j)

    # 2) Tile both the row (i) and column (j) dimensions.
    #    Conceptually transforms the fused loop nest into:
    #
    #    for I in [0, n) step TI:
    #      for J in [0, m) step TJ:
    #        for ii in [0, min(TI, n - I)):
    #          for jj in [0, min(TJ, m - J)):
    #            let i = I + ii, j = J + jj
    #            s[j] += A[i, j] * r[i]
    #            q[i] += A[i, j] * p[j]
    #
    # This improves cache locality for sub-tiles of A, p, q, and s.
    block(i, I, TI)
    block(j, J, TJ)

    # 3) Reorder the tile loops so we process one column-tile J at a time
    #    across all row-tiles I. This keeps the TJ-sized slices of p and s hot
    #    in cache while we stream through rows:
    #
    #    for J (outer):
    #      for I:
    #        for ii:
    #          for jj:
    #            ...
    hoist(J)
    hoist(I)

    # 4) Introduce tile-local accumulators to reduce global memory traffic:
    #
    #    - For each column tile J, we use s_tile[jj] (jj ∈ [0, TJ)) to hold the
    #      partial sum for s[J + jj] across all rows. We load s into s_tile once
    #      (or just zero it, since the spec initializes s to zero), update it
    #      entirely in the fast local buffer, then write back once per element.
    #
    #    - For each (I, J) tile, we use q_tile[ii] (ii ∈ [0, TI)) to hold the
    #      partial contribution to q[I + ii] coming from columns in the J-tile.
    #      After finishing jj for that tile, we accumulate q_tile into global q.
    #
    #    This transforms the inner part of the computation into the following
    #    structure (pseudocode):
    #
    #      # initialization (outside tiles)
    #      for j in [0, m): s[j] = 0
    #      for i in [0, n): q[i] = 0
    #
    #      for J in tiles of j:
    #        # tile-local s
    #        for jj in [0, TJ): s_tile[jj] = 0
    #        for I in tiles of i:
    #          # tile-local q
    #          for ii in [0, TI): q_tile[ii] = 0
    #          for ii in [0, min(TI, n - I)):
    #            i = I + ii
    #            r_i = r[i]
    #            for jj in [0, min(TJ, m - J)):
    #              j = J + jj
    #              a = A[i, j]
    #              s_tile[jj] += r_i * a
    #              q_tile[ii] += a * p[j]
    #          for ii in [0, min(TI, n - I)):
    #            q[I + ii] += q_tile[ii]
    #        for jj in [0, min(TJ, m - J)):
    #          s[J + jj] += s_tile[jj]
    #
    #    which is algebraically equivalent to the original S and Q definitions.
    introduce_local_buffer(s_tile[jj], s[J * TJ + jj])  # custom: stage s[J: J+TJ) into s_tile
    introduce_local_buffer(q_tile[ii], q[I * TI + ii])  # custom: accumulate q over TI rows locally

    # 5) Vectorize the innermost column loop over jj. Since A, p, s_tile, and
    #    the jj dimension are contiguous in memory, this corresponds to using
    #    SIMD loads/stores and FMA along the column-tile:
    #
    #      for ii:
    #        r_i = r[I + ii]
    #        vectorized for jj (width VJ):
    #          ...
    #
    #    VJ is chosen to match the hardware SIMD width (e.g., 4 or 8 for AVX).
    vectorize(jj, VJ)

    # 6) Parallelize over row tiles I (or equivalently over I×ii) to exploit
    #    multi-core parallelism. Updates to:
    #
    #      - q[I + ii] are reductions over tiles J;
    #      - s_tile[jj] are reductions over row tiles I;
    #
    #    so the implementation must treat these as reduction variables
    #    (e.g., per-thread accumulators or atomic additions), but no
    #    additional large buffers are required in this model.
    parallelize(I)
```

The Exo kernel computes two coupled matrix–vector products:

- `q = A * p`   (length `n`)
- `s = Aᵀ * r`  (length `m`)

while reusing each `A[i,j]` once.

Below is an optimized model description capturing this computation and a cache-/SIMD-/parallel-friendly schedule.

```text
domain:
    # Matrix A has shape [n, m]
    i: dim in [0, n)   # row index of A, and index of vectors r, q
    j: dim in [0, m)   # column index of A, and index of vectors p, s

data:
    # Row‑major matrix: A[i,j] laid out with j as fastest-varying index
    A[i, j]: in DATA_TYPE      = (i, j) -> i * m + j      # row-major
    p[j]:    in DATA_TYPE      = j       -> j             # length m
    r[i]:    in DATA_TYPE      = i       -> i             # length n
    q[i]: out    DATA_TYPE     = i       -> i             # length n
    s[j]: out    DATA_TYPE     = j       -> j             # length m

parameters:
    # Problem sizes:
    n: int   # number of rows of A, length of r, q
    m: int   # number of cols of A, length of p, s

    # Tunable schedule parameters (chosen for target machine):
    T_I: int   # tile size in i-dimension (e.g., 32–256, fits rows and q,r in L2)
    T_J: int   # tile size in j-dimension (e.g., 64–256, fits cols and p,s in L1)
    V_J: int   # SIMD vector width for j (e.g., 8 or 16 elements)
    U_J: int   # scalar unroll factor for j after vectorization (e.g., 2–4)

computation:
    # Mathematical definition of BiCG:
    #   s = Aᵀ r  and  q = A p
    #
    # Written as two reductions so that later scheduling is free to
    # reorder / fuse / tile loops as long as these sums are preserved.

    for j in [0, m):
        COMPUTE_S:
            s[j] = sum(i in [0, n), r[i] * A[i, j])

    for i in [0, n):
        COMPUTE_Q:
            q[i] = sum(j in [0, m), A[i, j] * p[j])

dependencies:
    # s and q depend only on inputs A, p, r and have no cross-dependence.
    # Thus the two computations can be reordered or fused freely.
    for j in [0, m):
        INPUTS -> COMPUTE_S(j)
    for i in [0, n):
        INPUTS -> COMPUTE_Q(i)

optimization:
    # 1. Fuse the two GEMV-like reductions so each A[i,j] is loaded once.
    #    After this, the conceptual loop nest becomes:
    #      for i in [0, n):
    #        for j in [0, m):
    #          s[j] += r[i] * A[i,j]
    #          q[i] += A[i,j] * p[j]
    #
    #    This preserves the mathematical sums defining s and q.
    fuse(COMPUTE_S, COMPUTE_Q)   # custom: fuse reductions over the shared A

    # 2. Tile both i and j dimensions to improve cache locality.
    #    Tiles (I, J) are chosen so that:
    #      - An I×J tile of A plus corresponding slices of p, r, q, s
    #        fit comfortably in L1/L2.
    #      - Extra temporary storage remains well under 50% of original.
    block(i, I, T_I)   # introduce outer tile index I and inner i
    block(j, J, T_J)   # introduce outer tile index J and inner j

    # 3. Keep tile loops I and J as the outermost loops to maximize
    #    reuse of tiles of A, p, r, q, s within each block.
    #    Resulting structure (conceptually):
    #      for I in seq(0, n) by T_I:
    #        for J in seq(0, m) by T_J:
    #          for i in I-tile:
    #            for j in J-tile:
    #              s[j] += r[i] * A[i,j]
    #              q[i] += A[i,j] * p[j]
    hoist(I)
    hoist(J)

    # 4. Within each tile, exploit SIMD and ILP along j, the contiguous dimension.
    #    A[i, j], p[j], and s[j] are laid out with contiguous j, so we
    #    vectorize the innermost j-loop and unroll it slightly for ILP.
    vectorize(j, V_J)   # map groups of V_J consecutive j's to SIMD lanes
    unroll(j, U_J)      # scalar unroll of the remaining loop body

    # 5. Parallelize across outer i-tiles (rows of A):
    #    - q[i] is a pure reduction over j for each fixed i; different i's
    #      are independent, so q can be written directly from each thread.
    #    - s[j] is a reduction over i. When parallelizing in i (or I),
    #      we must implement s as a parallel reduction:
    #        * each thread accumulates a private partial s_tile[j] for the
    #          J-tile it is working on, OR
    #        * threads use atomic adds to the shared s[j].
    #      A common choice is per-thread private s_tile of size T_J, then a
    #      serial or tree reduction into the final s after each tile.
    #
    #    The additional memory for private s_tile/p_tile buffers is at most:
    #       (#threads) * (T_J for s_tile + T_J for optional p_tile)
    #    which can be kept well below 50% of |A| + |p| + |r| + |q| + |s|
    #    by choosing T_J appropriately (e.g., T_J << m, and m << n·m = |A|).
    parallelize(I)      # distribute I-tiles across threads with reduction on s[j]

    # 6. (Optional, hardware-specific) Stage p and s tiles in fast memory.
    #    This can be modeled as:
    #      - allocate small on-stack buffers
    #          p_tile[T_J], s_tile[T_J]
    #      - copy p[J-tile] -> p_tile once per J-tile
    #      - accumulate into s_tile, then write back to s[J-tile]
    #    This further reduces cache misses on p and s while adding
    #    only O(T_J) extra storage per thread.
    #    We omit a formal directive here and treat it as a local
    #    implementation choice within the tiled, vectorized inner loops.
```

This model:

- Preserves the original BiCG semantics (`q = A p`, `s = Aᵀ r`).
- Reuses each `A[i,j]` once via loop fusion.
- Improves cache locality with 2D tiling over `(i, j)`.
- Exploits SIMD along the contiguous `j` dimension.
- Exposes outer `I` tiles for parallelization, with `s` handled as a reduction using thread-private tile buffers or atomics, keeping extra memory within the allowed budget.

```text
domain:
    i: dim in [0, N)          # row index
    j: dim in [0, M)          # column index

data:
    # Dense N x M matrix A in row-major layout.
    A[i, j]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * M + j

    # Input vectors.
    p[j]: in DATA_TYPE = j -> j          # length M
    r[i]: in DATA_TYPE = i -> i          # length N

    # Output vectors, fully overwritten by the kernel.
    s[j]: out DATA_TYPE = j -> j         # length M
    q[i]: out DATA_TYPE = i -> i         # length N

parameters:
    TJ:  size   # column tile size for cache/SIMD (e.g., 32–128, tuned)
    VEC: size   # SIMD width in elements (e.g., 8 for AVX2 f32, 4 for f64)
    T:   size   # number of threads used for parallelizing rows i

computation:
    # 1. Initialize s to zero over its M entries.
    #    This matches the explicit initialization loop in the Exo kernel.
    for j in [0, M):
        s[j] = 0.0

    # 2. Main BiCG computation:
    #    - For each row i, compute q[i] = sum_j A[i, j] * p[j].
    #    - Simultaneously accumulate into s[j] = sum_i r[i] * A[i, j].
    #    This is exactly the fused update in the Exo kernel:
    #        s[j] += r[i] * A[i, j]
    #        q[i] += A[i, j] * p[j]
    for i in [0, N):
        q[i] = 0.0
        for j in [0, M):
            s[j] += r[i] * A[i, j]
            q[i] += A[i, j] * p[j]

optimization:
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Initialization of s
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # The s-initialization loop is fully independent across j.
    # We parallelize and vectorize it to hide its (small) cost.
    parallelize(j)              # over the j-loop in s[j] = 0.0
    vectorize(j, VEC)

    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
    # Main i,j loop over A, p, r producing s and q
    # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

    # 1. Tile the inner column loop to improve cache locality for A and s and
    #    to align iteration with SIMD width.
    #
    # Original nest:
    #   for i in [0, N):
    #     q[i] = 0
    #     for j in [0, M):
    #       s[j] += r[i] * A[i, j]
    #       q[i] += A[i, j] * p[j]
    #
    # After blocking j:
    #   for i in [0, N):
    #     q[i] = 0
    #     for J in [0, ceil(M / TJ)):
    #       for j in [J*TJ, min((J+1)*TJ, M)):
    #         ...
    #
    # A remains row-major; each inner j-tile traverses A[i, j] and s[j] contiguously.
    block(j, J, TJ)             # j = J * TJ + j_in, with tiles of TJ columns
    hoist(J)                    # outer structure: for i ... for J ... for j_in_tile ...

    # 2. Vectorize within each column tile.
    #
    # The inner j-loop is a good SIMD candidate:
    #   - s[j] updates are independent across j within a fixed i.
    #   - q[i] is a scalar reduction over j and can use a SIMD horizontal sum.
    #   - A[i, j], p[j], and s[j] are contiguous in memory.
    vectorize(j, VEC)           # j here is the inner (tiled) column index

    # 3. Exploit parallelism over rows i.
    #
    # Semantics:
    #   q[i] = sum_j A[i, j] * p[j]          (reduction over j, local to i)
    #   s[j] = sum_i r[i] * A[i, j]          (reduction over i, shared across rows)
    #
    # Therefore:
    #   - Rows i are independent for q (each q[i] uses only row i).
    #   - s[j] is a reduction over i; all contributions to s[j] are additive.
    #
    # We parallelize over i and implement s as a reduction variable:
    #   - Each thread t allocates a private partial sum s_t[j], initialized to 0.
    #   - It processes its subset of rows i, updating q[i] directly and s_t[j].
    #   - At the end, we perform a final reduction:
    #         s[j] = sum_{t=0..T-1} s_t[j].
    #
    # Extra memory:
    #   - Additional storage is T * M * sizeof(DATA_TYPE) for the s_t buffers.
    #   - The dominant storage is A (N * M elements), so for typical N >> T
    #     this is far below a 50% increase in total memory footprint.
    parallelize(i)              # parallel over i with reduction on s[j] across threads

    # 4. The scalar reduction q[i] over j and the reduction s[j] over i
    #    are left to the low-level compiler to exploit FMA and horizontal
    #    SIMD reductions; the loop blocking and vectorization hints above
    #    ensure contiguous access and high arithmetic intensity while
    #    preserving the original BiCG kernel’s semantics (modulo standard
    #    floating-point associativity differences).
```
